Strake
STRAYK
verb (past tense)
The older past tense of strike, from the Saxon strican. In Act 27:17 the phrase strake sail is the seaman’s idiom for striking — that is, lowering — the sail, the same sense in which a ship strikes her colours.

Biblical Definition

“Which when they had taken up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven” (Act 27:17). The verse is the turning point of the greatest sea narrative in Scripture. Caught by the tempestuous wind Euroclydon (Act 27:14), the crew do everything seamanship allows: they take up the boat, they frap the hull with cables to keep her from breaking apart, and then they lower the sail — the last resort, the surrender of all steering — and are driven. To strike sail is to stop trying to make headway and let the storm carry you. For fourteen days they drift, and the narrative records that all hope was taken away. It is precisely there, when the ship is being driven and every competence has been exhausted, that Paul stands forth and says, “be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me” (Act 27:25). Two things sit together in this chapter and must not be separated. Every measure of ordinary seamanship is used, energetically and to the last; and the deliverance, when it comes, is by promise and not by seamanship. God had told Paul that not a soul would be lost, and not a soul was — and they still had to keep the sailors from escaping in the boat.

Webster 1828 Definition

The older past tense of strike; in the phrase strake sail, to lower the sail in a storm, surrendering headway and letting the ship be driven.

expand to see more

STRIKE, v.t. To lower; to let down; as, to strike sail, or to strike a flag.

STRAKE, the old past tense of strike; Saxon strican.

To strike sail is to lower the sails, in submission, in salute, or in stress of weather.

Figuratively, to yield; to abate pretensions; to acknowledge a superior.

Act 27:17: they strake sail, and so were driven before the tempest.

Key Scripture

Act 27:14 — "But not long after there arose against it a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon."

Act 27:17 — "Which when they had taken up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven."

Act 27:20 — "And when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away."

Act 27:25 — "Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me."

Modern Corruption

Providence is habitually set against effort, so that trusting God is imagined to mean ceasing to work — while Acts 27 shows a crew frapping the hull and cutting away the boat inside an absolute divine promise.

expand to see more

The corruption is the false alternative between faith and means. It takes two forms, and Acts 27 rebukes both. The first says that if God has promised, effort is superfluous — let go, let God, and stop striving. The second says that since the sea is indifferent and the ship is real, seamanship is all there is, and prayer is a gesture. Luke, who was aboard, records neither. He records cables under the hull, tackling thrown overboard, soundings taken, four anchors cast out of the stern, and a wheat cargo jettisoned — alongside an angel of God standing by Paul in the night with an unconditional word: God hath given thee all them that sail with thee.

Recover the plain sense: the sharpest illustration is Act 27:31. God had promised that not one life would be lost, and when the sailors tried to flee in the boat Paul said, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved — and the soldiers cut the ropes and let her fall off. The promise was certain and the means were necessary, and Paul saw no contradiction whatever between them. God ordains ends and means together, which is why the doctrine of providence has never in Reformed hands produced fatalism. Strike sail when seamanship is exhausted; keep sounding, keep praying, keep the crew aboard; and be of good cheer on the ground Paul names — not because the storm looks survivable, but for I believe God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon strican, the old past tense of strike — to lower sail; the surrender of headway inside an unbroken promise.

expand to see more

Strake — the older past tense of strike; Saxon strican.

To strike sail is the seaman’s idiom for lowering the sail.

The same idiom gives striking a flag or colours — a token of submission.

Act 27:17: the last resort, after undergirding the ship with helps.

Act 27:20: neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and all hope was taken away.

Usage

"To strike sail is to give up headway and be driven — the end of seamanship."

"Act 27:31: the promise was absolute and the means were still necessary."

"Paul’s ground of cheer is not the weather but I believe God."
